newsitem.title: USA: Jazz finally wins Pulitzer Prize for music.
newsitem.headline: Jazz finally wins Pulitzer Prize for music.

text.p: Journalists whose subjects ranged from the war in Afghanistan to the battle against AIDS won Pulitzer prizes on Monday and for the first time the 80-year-old awards for excellence paid homage to a working jazz musician.

No award was given for drama for the first time since 1986, although the drama committee recommended three plays and a minority committee came up with its own candidate. The Pulitzer board said none of the candidates met its standards. It was the 14th time since 1917 that no drama award was given.

An American raised in Ireland, Frank McCourt, a 66-year-old retired schoolteacher, won the prize for biography for "Angela's Ashes," a searing story of growing up poor, starving and sick in Limerick. Novelist Steven Millhauser won the prize for fiction for "Martin Dressler," described as the decline and fall of one man's quest for the American dream.

Trumpet virtuoso Wynton Marsalis, 35, won the prize for music for his three-hour oratorio with jazz orchestra, "Blood on the Fields," which tells of an African king thrown into slavery in the United States.

Pulitzer administrator Seymour Topping said it was the first time a work of jazz and blues-inflected music won the award. The Pulitzer board in 1965 had rejected a special citation recommended for Edward "Duke" Ellington.
It was the second consecutive year that a black musician won. Last year it was classical composer George Walker for "Lilacs."
The prizes in journalism, drama, letters and music are awarded annually on the recommendation of the Pulitzer Prize Board at Columbia University.
The prize for general non-fiction went to "Ashes to Ashes: America's 100-Year Cigarette War, the Public Health, and the Unabashed Triumph of Philip Morris," by Richard Kluger.
The prize for poetry went to Lisel Mueller for "Alive Together: New and Selected Poems."
In the journalism awards, the spot news reporting prize was awarded to Newsday's staff in Melville, New York, for its coverage of the TWA Flight 800 crash and its aftermath.

The Wall Street Journal staff won for national reporting for its coverage of the struggle against AIDS. The paper broke the story that a cocktail of drugs was proving effective in controlling the virus that causes AIDS.

John F. Burns of The New York Times won for international reporting for the second time; in 1993 he won for his reporting from Bosnia. This year he was cited "for his courageous and insightful coverage of the harrowing regime imposed on Afghanistan by the Taliban."
The feature photography prize went to Alexander Zemlianichenko of the Associated Press for his photo of Russian President Boris Yeltsin dancing at a rock concert during his re-election campaign.
